research_thread.scientific_problem: Refractory High-Entropy Alloys (RHEAs) face a trade-off where beneficial oxidation-resistant elements (Al, Cr, Si) simultaneously promote brittle intermetallic phase formation, potentially compromising mechanical integrity at high temperatures.
research_thread.material_system: W-V-Ta-Ti-Cr (WVTaTiCrx) Refractory High-Entropy Alloy coatings on 42-CrMo steel substrate.
research_thread.sample_lineage: Laser cladded powder mixture (W, V, Ta, Ti, Cr) solidified into a BCC solid-solution matrix with precipitating Laves phases.
research_thread.intervention: Incremental addition of Chromium (Cr) content (x = 0 to 1) in the WVTaTiCrx system.
research_thread.conditions: Laser cladding processing (1.4 kW, 8 mm/s), followed by high-temperature oxidation (800°C, air, 50h) and corrosion testing (NaCl solution).
research_thread.structure: Primary BCC solid-solution dendrites enriched with W, Ta; interdendritic regions with V, Cr; precipitation of Cr2Ta Laves phase increasing with Cr content.
research_thread.outcome: Increased Cr content significantly improved hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance (lower rate), and corrosion resistance (higher potential, lower rate), attributed to denser passive films and slower atomic diffusion due to lattice distortion.
research_thread.mechanism: Cr addition increases lattice distortion, slowing atomic diffusion and binding speed with oxygen to form denser oxide films; simultaneously reduces BCC phase stability via small enthalpy of mixing, promoting Laves phase precipitation.
alternative_explanations: The improved mechanical properties are due solely to solid-solution strengthening rather than microstructural refinement, despite Laves phase precipitation.
boundaries: Cr content increase promotes Laves phase formation which may eventually lead to embrittlement at higher concentrations not yet tested (e.g., x > 1).

evidence_spans: Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ].

The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ].
Unfortunately, elements Al, Cr, and Si very easily form brittle intermetallic compounds with other refractory elements, resulting in reduced mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [14] , [15] , [16] ].
W and Ta elements have adequate mechanical properties and resistance to irradiation-induced embrittlement and swelling [ [22] ].
Ti plays a significant role in improving the sintered density [ [19] ], whereas V aids in improving the strength and hardness of refractory HEAs [ [23] ].
Another refractory metal, Cr was also chosen for use, considering its ability for high-temperature oxidation [ [24] , [25] , [26] , [27] ].

The high-entropy alloys undergo segregation when prepared by melting, and embrittlement and porosity are attributes of conventional sintering, whereas the low thickness of the final product is a limit of the physical vapor deposition (PVD) approach [ [28] ].
In addition, electrodeposition techniques lead to pores and microcracks in the coating [ [29] ].

Compared with magnetron sputtering, PTA welding, and additive manufacturing, the research shows that the cladding layer forms firm metallurgical bonds with the substrate, the heat-affected zone of the coating is small, the deformation of the substrate is small, and the coating thickness can reach the millimeter level [ [30] ].

At the same time, the enthalpy of mixing formed between Cr and other refractory elements is small, which reduces the enthalpy value in the alloy and the stability of the BCC phase, which leads to the precipitation of the Laves phase.
